Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber has carefully followed the development of the cross-examination as -- has looked at what areas you wanted to explore in much, much detail, what you wanted to do as far as listening for 16 minutes to a portion of a transcript which is already in evidence. We have also considered that a number of questions you wanted to put to the witness were read out but they were not answered. That saves time. The Chamber has decided that you have one hour left for your cross-examination, which will start in -- the remainder will start in 20 minutes from now after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I remind Your Honours that the Prosecution was granted additional time even though they didn't ask for it? And I would like for there to be equality of arms, Your Honours. All these questions are relevant. All these matters are relevant. There's not a single portion that I have gone through that is not precisely relevant to this case and the witness's credibility or our allegations of his lack of credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I have said before, the Chamber has considered the way in which you conducted your cross-examination, has, of course, included the relevance, the level of relevance, the time spent on certain matters, the time also spent on matters where the witness apparently was totally unaware of. Not to say that that's always irrelevant, but this is the decision the Chamber has taken on the matter. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, I see you're on your feet. I'd like to say one more word before the witness comes into the courtroom. If Mr. Ivetic wants to draw our attention to the fact that the Baxter report may have ignored relevant information which was available, which is a relevant point to raise, and if he will suggest in the questions that the witness was to be blamed for relying on such a report, that can be done in seven minutes instead of taking ages and ages for that. That is the major issue apart from a few others I mentioned. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Still, I know that Mr. Ivetic has a lot of documents to go through with this witness, and we were leaning on your guidances, Your Honours. Respectfully, you have said for 92 ter witnesses that the Prosecution has half an hour. We know that the Prosecution for this witness used 2 hours and 43 minutes. If we go in maths, it would be more than 12 hours for our cross-examination. All we ask is to have the remaining of these two hours so Mr. Ivetic can go through all the documents he has to go through. And there is one video he has to go through. The Prosecution was able to introduce some audios by just proposing them, but we have to ask the witness about this video, and we are not going to go through the audios we mentioned before, but if you allow us, we can shorten the time as well by having this video played only once if it's possible to have it translated immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That, of course, depends on the situation, but -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists the Chamber, as it stands now I have no redirect for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No redirect, which certainly gives some additional time, which ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now aware that there would be more time available, which depending on how the time is used may become available to Mr. Ivetic. So the ruling stands at this moment, but there's a fair chance that the extra time remaining may become available to Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, my initial observation stands firmly, if I could say so. It's a matter of how to point at issues you want to make. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to move along to another topic, humanitarian convoys. At paragraph 41 of your statement, which is P785 MFI, page 10 in the English, page 8 in the B/C/S, you talk about how General Mladic demanded reciprocity in the delivery of aid, i.e., that for every convoy allowed into the enclaves, one should be equally delivered to the Serbs. Why were you and UNPROFOR treating the parties differently as to the distribution of aid so as not to agree to an equal distribution as proposed by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR did not distribute aid. That was the UNHCR. UNPROFOR's business was to -- to protect the convoys and see -- and see that they got delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to take a look at -- well, various points of your statement. For instance, at paragraph 50, which is page 12 in the English, and page 8 in the B/C/S, you complain of detailed searches of aid vehicles. Would you agree with me that given the concerns of smuggling, such searches were appropriate and justified by the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just looking at where I'm supposed to have complained.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 50, sir. "I can't remember whether it was on my way out or in --"

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I can understand very well while -- why the -- Mladic and his forces wanted to search the convoys. Nevertheless, that caused considerable delay and in some cases things, material and so forth, was taken off them by the searchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that arms were reaching the ABiH forces through humanitarian aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that it had happened. Whether it happened in the year I was in command, I don't know, and I don't think it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can look at 1D605.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as we wait for that document to come up on the screen, I think we'll see it as a one-page document. From the date it is the 29th of May, 1993. From the stamp on the bottom left it is from the Bosnian embassy in Zagreb to the commander of the BiH 5th Corps in Bihac. The document discusses various military gear that is listed, and it is identified that it will be sent via a vehicle identified as UNHCR 103709. First of all, sir, looking at this list of -- of military materiel and ammunition, would you agree that the amounts are rather significant?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's plenty of ammunition there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have a time frame for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's 1993, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's outside the scope of -- that the amount is significant, the Chamber can see that. I mean, has the witness any knowledge about this incident? Then we can ask him questions about it. He said, "I know that it happened in the past." He's not aware of it happening during his tenure. Is there any disagreement, Mr. Groome, about this document as that this reported, apart from whether it arrived or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't find any record of this document in my our system, so I'd be unprepared to agree to the information contained in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's -- let's try to elicit from the witness evidence he can give rather than whether 3.570 pieces of EKs is significant, yes or no. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems high number. Yes. Bullets, 50.000, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, a few moments ago you told me that you did have knowledge of -- that it happened prior to your time. Would this be the type of information that you had of incidents prior to your tenure as BH commander when UNHCR vehicles were utilised by the ABiH to smuggle weapons into its forces in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no such information such as and this doesn't actually say it happened. The -- the -- I think what I had been told was something to the effect that it had happened and this was one of the reasons why the UN in the past had agreed to convoys being searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to look at something from your time period. It is 65 ter number 25915. It is a Prosecution 65 ter document for which unfortunately in e-court I could not find the English translation, although I do know that one exists as I have seen one, but I would like to just read for you the first paragraph and ask you about this. This is, first of all, 12th of May, 1995, and the first paragraph in B/C/S reads as follows, and hopefully you'll get the translation: [Interpretation] "Based on the available information, the members of UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and other international organisations are illegally transporting fuel for the needs of the Muslims in the following enclaves: Sarajevo, Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. They smuggled the fuel in double-bottom tanks and tanks which are bigger than usual in combat and noncombat vehicles. They then empty these tanks in the enclaves and leave smaller amounts of fuel in the tanks which is sufficient for the return from the enclaves into the territory of the FRY and the RS." [In English] Sir, were these kinds of allegations brought to your attention during your tenure as BH commander?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this particular correspondence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct you to paragraph 92 of your statement. You seem to identify that General Gvero had complained to you that the UN in Srebrenica were supplying fuel to the defenders. I'm asking about this type of information, not this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. Then, yes, I can -- that -- that this was alleged to have happened I heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you undertake any steps to try and stop such activities?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I set out to find out whether it was happening or not, and I don't recall that I found any evidence that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If I can look at paragraph 32 of your statement, which is P785 MFI'd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do that, just some clarification from you, please. At paragraph -- at page 57, line 15 to 16, you asked the question: "Were you aware that arms were reaching the ABiH forces through humanitarian convoys," and in support of that you showed this exhibit that's on the screen coming from Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, I do not see from the document, and if you could help me I'd appreciate it, from the face of the document how it is linked to being -- to this consignment being transported through aid convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the vehicle identified has a UNHCR number. The witness had testified the UNHCR was doing the aid convoys, and perhaps we can ask the witness if, in fact, the UNHCR vehicles, as part of convoys, would have had these designations as UNHCR registration numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the UNHCR number, is it here on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the end of the list. At the end of the list it says the vehicle has UNHCR registration number which I read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that we were not shown the second page? This is on the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm looking at the page that we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I had that it was a one-page document in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your suggestion is that it was a UNHCR vehicle which was used and, for example, not false plates being used on another vehicle. That's -- Mr. Ivetic, I'm just trying to understand your questioning and the probative value of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this is a document that I haven't tendered because this witness said he didn't have knowledge of this particular incident. I was exploring his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking whether it was part of the suggestion in your question that the mentioning of this number would be that UNHCR vehicles were used or that you also considered the possibility that false plates were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There are other possibilities as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Fine. Then that's clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we're -- I apologise. I intended to call up your statement, P785, marked for identification, paragraph 32, which is page 8 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S. And I will be dealing with the English wherein you state: "The Bosnian Army was making open preparations to fight on in the spring. UNPROFOR observed and were told by the Bosnian Serbs that one the air trips at Tuzla was being used at night. Mladic alluded to this during the course of the meeting. Investigating these events caused a degree of friction between NATO and the United Nations." What I want to ask you is what was the friction between NATO and the United Nations about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what we'd seen. The argument that was going on was that the -- NATO no-fly zone was a -- should have been able to see these aircraft, and so why didn't we know about them. We'd seen one at least either just landing or -- I think it was just taking off. I can't remember the exact situation. And as it was about the same time as this meeting with General Mladic had taken place and we'd -- and he'd told me these things were happening. And we were being told that they -- it was -- then we hadn't seen any aeroplanes. What we were seeing was lights of aeroplanes going in to land at Belgrade and other things, and there was this disagreement running between the organisation on the ground and the organisation in the air, if you like. Between the UN on the ground and NATO in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it also part of the observations of the UN observers that the Bosnian Muslim forces utilising helicopters which they had painted white to mimic UNPROFOR helicopters were then transporting arms and munitions from Tuzla airport to the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think we did observe that, and we didn't observe any helicopters other than our own painted white.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at 1D601 briefly. And while we wait for that, I believe it's dated the 14th of February, 1995, and the cover page indicates it's a letter from General Mladic to commander -- or pardon me, for General Smith. If we can go to the second page of the same. And if we could take a look at it. This indicates: "Dear General, we are gravely concerned over the frequent use of Tuzla airport by the Muslim side. The aircrafts are bringing weapons, ammunition, and war materials for their needs. "Unfortunately, this pirate activity of their aircraft is enabled by the NATO Air Force, and the Muslim army does not allow your forces to control the roads -- the loads," pardon me. "I'm sure you share my opinion that these activities are seriously jeopardising the signed agreements and represent a serious breach of the truce and of relevant Security Council Resolutions. "I ask you to take urgent measures to stop these peace-threatening activities, otherwise we will be compelled to take the necessary measures regarding the Muslim side's violations of the Tuzla safe area, which is, in the presence of your forces, turning into a war base for Islamic countries." If I can ask you, sir, do you recall having received this protest letter from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that these complaints from General Mladic were substantiated?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw it. I just told you this. We -- we -- at about the time this letter is arriving, I am receiving reports of an aeroplane having been seen and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document as the next available 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D601 shall be assigned Exhibit D140. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D140 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned strife between NATO and the UN, am I correct that there was a particular party within NATO that was more vociferously supporting calls for arming the Muslims and that that was the United States of America?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say strife. I said a degree of friction between NATO and the United Nations, and I am not referring to their political bodies. I am referring to the deployed elements of those forces in and over Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 1D600 in e-court. While we wait for that, sir, I think you'll see this to be dated the 12th of February, 1995, from the -- I believe from the Norwegian battalion of UNPROFOR. Am I correct that the -- there was a Norwegian battalion of UNPROFOR at Tuzla air base.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mixed, if I remember correctly, a Nordic battalion. There were Danes, Norwegians and Swedes in the grouping.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second page of this document, and the general overview I'd like to focus on the middle of the paragraph and the portion that begins: "Late Friday night an aircraft was observed flying at low altitude over the area east of Tuzla with every indication it was going to land. It was assumed this would happen in Tuzla east where there is --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "... where there is an extended highway stretch. The UN APCs which were sent out to investigate the matter were prevented by the BiH, Bosnia-Herzegovina army, from doing so. It therefore cannot be confirmed whether the aircraft actually landed or not or whether a load was dropped at low altitude." Sir, you indicated that your forces had seen -- is this the same incident that you recall or is it a different one?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is the indent I'm referring and it's coincidental with the letter that you showed me earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR lodge any complaints with the BiH side as to the actions of its soldiers in preventing UNPROFOR from investigating?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you threaten air strikes against the BiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on that occasion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How often it during your tenure did events like this one occur as to -- as to Tuzla airport?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember one where other than this one, but there were, I think, one or two other cases in -- with airstrips in the general area of south of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could tender this document as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D600 shall be assigned Exhibit D141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to call up 1D603.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, I believe the date of this document is the 24th of February, 1995, so several days after the one that we just looked at. And this appears to be sent to -- sent by the -- by the UNMOs to their UNMO headquarters, and it is identified as a protest letter for General Mladic, and it is sent to General de Lapresle and General Smith. Having looked at this, do you recall having received this protest letter during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this isn't the protest letter. I'm not -- I'm not understanding. Does this cover a protest letter, or is this in front of me the protest letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding that this is the protest letter.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could would have a look at the top. It reads: "Note: Signature is not General Mladic. BSA headquarters only advised us that it is the signature of another General ..." which seems to indicate that this may be just a copy sent, but when -- I interpreted this wrong, then please explain what -- could we have a look at the remainder of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I believe is this is a retransmission of a translation of a document that would have been originally in B/C/S sent through the UNMO structure to make its way to the various identified recipients, but we can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if he knows. I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am -- I am confident that I would have seen this. I just don't remember. Letters such as this would have been shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask for the top of the document to be shown perhaps that could help assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The fax header indicates -- whoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can stay on that page. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The fax header indicates BH FWD com send. Would that be BH forward command centre?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's gone into the UNMOs, as I see it, and then being asked to pass to commander -- BH command's office, and I'm sure they did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why they wouldn't have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. With regard to this document, if we can look at what is detailed therein. "On 23 February, 1995, at about 2010 hours, a transport plane with weapons and military equipment landed again at Tuzla airport's secondary runway. It was escorted by 2 NATO fighter aircraft which were protecting it during flight and off-loading. "Unfortunately, this has been repeated lately in front (within sight and hearing) of NATO and UNPROFOR forces both in the air and at Tuzla airport itself. These forces are doing nothing to prevent the violation of the relevant UN Security Council Resolutions prohibiting the import of weapons and military equipment." Do you recall hearing of this type of incident where the planes were actually being escorted by NATO fighter jets?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was never part of the -- my understanding of what had been happened, what I'd been told had been going on. And I -- and I only remember, as I've said to you before, the one case of the aeroplane appearing to be about to land or having just taken off from Tuzla. Maybe other ones were heard in the vicinity. I don't know. Maybe it would have occurred on other days. Again, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document as the next available 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just reserve my position for a few minutes? I'll perhaps rise at a convenient moment and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a number should be assigned to it. We'll then delay the decision on admission. Mr. Registrar, the number reserved for this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D603 shall be assigned D142.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. I can say now we do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D142 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to now return to your statement, P785 MFI'd, paragraph 23, which is at page 6 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. And here, sir, the selection I want to focus on is the part that says: "The federation forced back into a relatively small area was beginning to gain strength. Their numerical superiority and the arms they were now getting would give them an advantage if they started to fight again." And I want to ask you, sir, your reference to the arms they were now getting, what is this a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were getting weapons in that I was aware of over the Dalmatian coast and were -- and were being fairly open about it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was this -- well, first of all, what kind of arms are we talking about, both heavy and infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My understanding was that they were primarily infantry weapons. They were not heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were they coming from somewhere outside of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never very clear about their provenance, but they were -- I understood that they were coming up out of Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the weapons coming from the Dalmatian coast and the suspected shipments coming through Tuzla airport. What did Lieutenant-Colonel Powers, your intelligence officer with links to the both NATO and US intelligence communities, have to say about these rumours or these allegations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it. He collated the information and so forth. I think this was collected by us observing the improvement in the weapons of the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you feel that you had an affirmative duty to try and keep weapons from coming into Sarajevo to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a duty to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How about the enclaves like Srebrenica? Do you feel you had an affirmative duty to keep weapons from coming into the enclaves to the BiH forces?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a duty to interfere directly with any of the armed forces provided they were not preventing me in carrying out my mandate of the delivery of humanitarian aid and so forth. And secondly, the safe area and exclusion zone policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about the ABiH forces inside safe areas and enclaves. Do you consider that UNPROFOR had an affirmative duty to demilitarise those forces and those zones?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. What they did was when the exclusion zone regime was established, weapon collection points for both sides were established, and they were established within Sarajevo and in Srebrenica where there were some -- not many, but some heavier weapons, and these were collected into weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 1D581 in e-court. This is another document that appears to have been communicated via the UNMO structure to the office of General Smith. It appears to be dated the 10th of July, albeit being transmitted by the UNMOs the 11th of July, 1995, and it purports again to be a letter from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to read for you the first paragraph and see if you recall this document. "I have received your letter from 9 July 1995. The Srebrenica enclave has not been demilitarised according to the agreements of 19 April and 8 May 1993. The Muslims have not handed over the weapons, mine/explosive and combative means to UNPROFOR. The Muslim forces have abused the special status of the safe area and presence of your forces for preparing and performing of terrorist and other fighting activities against Serb population and the territory of the Republic of Srpska." Do you recall having received this letter during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing this letter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, General Mladic details the killings of various civilians in the surrounding villages of the safe area by the Muslim forces. Did you have knowledge and information about these attacks by the Muslims from within Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not allowed into the Bosnian Serb territory to investigate anything such as this, so, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you threaten air strikes against the ABiH forces for their violations of the demilitarisation agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And the air strikes -- and this agreement that you refer to I'd have to check, but I don't think that has anything to do with the -- with the exclusion zones, and the exclusion zones did not cover small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph of this document indicates that several -- that UNPROFOR members -- that one UNPROFOR soldier was killed by the Muslims. Are you aware of that incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were air strikes considered and/or threatened in self-defence by UNPROFOR against the ABiH forces for the killing of the UNPROFOR soldier?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for this document to be introduced into evidence as the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D581 shall be assigned Exhibit D143. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would call up 65 ter number 17956 from the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, this is an agreement for the demilitarisation of Srebrenica which is from April of 1993. April 18th is the date that it was signed per the second page wherein we have signatures of General Halilovic, General Mladic, and General Wahlgren. First of all, are you familiar with General Wahlgren? Was he a predecessor within UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I'm not sure. Did he follow General Morillon? I'm not -- I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe he was there around the same time as General Morillon. If I could direct your attention to item number 4. "The demilitarisation of Srebrenica will be complete within 72 hours of the arrival of the UNPROFOR company in Srebrenica (1100 hours 18 April 1993, if they arrive later this will be changed). All weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives, and combat supplies (except medicines) inside Srebrenica will be submitted/handed over to UNPROFOR under the supervision of three officers from each side with control carried out by UNPROFOR. No armed persons or units except UNPROFOR will remain within the city once the demilitarisation process is complete. Responsibility for the demilitarisation process remains with UNPROFOR." Sir, looking at this agreement, would you agree that it places an affirmative responsibility upon UNPROFOR with respect to the demilitarisation process in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the rest of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mean the second page?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second page.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And was this agreement -- I don't recall the history at this time. Was this agreement ratified --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- by the -- by Halilovic's superiors?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir, whether this document and its language the responsibility for the demilitarisation process remains with UNPROFOR, whether it presents an affirmative responsibility on the part of UNPROFOR with respect to the demilitarisation process of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm not answering you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness says, "I would like to know whether this is was what the status of this agreement is." There are two questions. The first one is does the text say? We can read that. It's fine if the witness agrees with us on what the text reads. The question you put was not limited to the text but whether it imposes an affirmative duty, and there the witness says not knowing exactly the status of this document, I have difficulties in answering your question. And then to say to the witness, "I asked you this. Answer that," seems not to be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not what the witness said. If you're going to interpret what the witness said, I can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was asking my question. If the witness has that to say, let him answer it, Your Honours. The witness said -- asked me a question. I believe witnesses are not allowed to ask counsel questions, Your Honour. If I'm wrong, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness needs further information before he thinks he can answer a question, then he certainly is allowed to ask further information. He is not questioning you, Mr. Ivetic, but let me read literally again what he said in the transcript. He said, "Was that agreement," and he then he said, "I don't recall the history of this. Was this agreement ratified by Halilovic's superiors?," which can reasonably only be understood as information the witness needs before he can answer the question. That is my reading of the witness's answer. Is that what you intended to say, Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm trying to establish -- here we have three parties to this agreement. Everybody has to be in agreement for this agreement to be operative, and I wanted to know whether that was the case before answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood your answer. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the previous document we looked at referenced this agreement. General Smith says he received the previous document. So the person that asked for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may put your next question to the witness. You have an opportunity to do now because you're limited in your time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing the document you've got up on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was referenced in the letter from General Mladic sent to you on the 10th of July, 1995. Would it have been your course and conduct as BH commander when a warring party indicated a violation of a particular agreement, would you not have investigated within your office to obtain a copy of agreement and to obtain all the history of the agreement to see whether in fact it was in force or not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at the time this document was received I am dealing with the aftermath of the collapse of the Srebrenica pocket, first point. Second point is that I would have asked the same question of this document that was referenced if I had seen it at the time. What is its status?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you advised when you assumed command of BH command that the enclaves were supposed to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up P023, an exhibit tendered by the Prosecution. And while we wait for that, sir, we will see that it is dated the 8th of May, 1993. So it's after this document that we looked at, and it relates to the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica. If we were to look at the last page of the same, we would see that it is signed by Generals Mladic, Halilovic, and Morillon. You had earlier mentioned -- asked me if the other document was related to General Morillon. Are you familiar with this document that is signed by General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I asked you is whether General Wahlgren had succeeded General Morillon, and you thought he was there at much the same time. This one, can I see the front page? You've given me the back page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If we can go back to the front.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not immediately, no. Let me read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you're ready to move on to the second page, I'd like to focus on that page and the matters contained therein.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. You can turn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page. And in particular I'd like to focus on Article 3. "Every military or paramilitary unit will have to either withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit/hand over their weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives, and combat supplies in the demilitarised zones will be handed over/submitted to UNPROFOR." Then it gives times for that, and Article 5 again says UNPROFOR shall control the demilitarised zone. The last two paragraphs of that article. "Noncombatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone, except members of UNPROFOR, are not permitted to have in their possession any weapon, ammunition or explosives. Weapons, ammunition, and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR." The question I have for you, sir: You had said earlier that you didn't believe that the -- that in the zones small arms were included. Does this agreement, not getting into now whether in fact it was being enforced, but does this agreement cover or seem to cover small arms in addition to heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But again, I question the status of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that you do, sir. During -- let me ask you this way: During the time-period when you were BH commander, were DutchBat units in Srebrenica tasked with attempting to demilitarise the area of Srebrenica according to your knowledge and information?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, I'd like to ask you to take a look at Exhibit P57, the statement of one of the DutchBat who was in Srebrenica Eelco Koster. And if we can turn to the sixth page of the same in the English. My questions will be very brief. The third paragraph from the top is dealing with the situation in mid-June and the patrols in Srebrenica, and the second half of that paragraph reads as follows: "It struck me that each time we turned out there were more Muslim fighters in the town than before. At that time we were no longer able to fulfil the policy requirements of the demilitarised zone. By this I mean that there were so many Muslim fighters walking about armed that we UN soldiers were incapable of disarming these people." Does that refresh your recollection, sir, that there was some kind of demilitarisation agreement that the DutchBat in Srebrenica were supposed to be enforcing?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I don't -- it was -- the -- the Bosnian forces inside the safe area, I don't recall at any stage in my time being expected to be demilitarised. Their heavy weapons, such as they were, were held, and were in Srebrenica, held in a weapon or weapon collection points, but -- and I don't recall that the safe areas were ever expected to be -- have completely disarmed people other than the UN inside them. That might have been a goal in 1992 or 1993, but it certainly wasn't the case at the beginning of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, may I ask the witness for one clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For his observation. We have seen two agreements, both signed by General Mladic and General Halilovic. And then we saw on the bottom "Witnessed by," and then there was the signature of an UNPROFOR general, Morillon and Wahlgren. What is your understanding of the word "witnessed by"? What status had, with respect to these documents, UNPROFOR has to play?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's perhaps how I should have answered an earlier question in that my understanding is that there are three parties to this agreement. There are the two making the agreement and the UNPROFOR general, in each case a different one, is witnessing this agreement. He can -- in other words, he can only carry out those duties that appear to be laid upon him provided the other two are playing their part in this agreement. He -- his activity is utterly dependent upon the agreement of the other two. That's what I understood those documents to be signed as and hence my question about their status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we could return to the witness statement of Mr. Koster. You had indicated, I believe, that this might have been from an earlier period but certainly not the beginning of 1995. If I can refer you to the first page -- pardon me, the second page of this document in e-court, we see that Mr. Koster was deployed 21st January, 1995, to Srebrenica, and so the entirety of this witness statement would relate to the time period after the 21st of January, 1995. And I want to ask you based upon what you knew on the ground, apart from being ordered to do so, where would Mr. Koster as part of DutchBat have gotten into his head the notion that he was supposed to be demilitarising Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure he's saying that. And if I understood the -- if we can go right back to the beginning, I'd want to know who he is. What's his role in this -- in his force?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it says right there, sir.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, he's a lieutenant. Right. And he's a logistic officer. Yes. Okay. I can -- I don't know him. I don't know how this was recorded, and I don't read Dutch, so I can't do it in the original, but he may have just been using the word "demilitarised zone" in a very general sense to describe the safe area or exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we still have the English version of the statement up of Mr. Koster up on the screen, I'd like to call up on the other half of the screen Exhibit P00038, which was discussed with the witness on -- last week during direct examination. And once that document is up on the -- on the left, if you could focus on the first page and item number 5. Sir, if you might recall, you were asked about this document and the paragraph 5, and you indicated that the DutchBat were not allowed into the Bandera Triangle by the VRS. I would like to further explore this with you, and I want to first read the relevant portion of paragraph 5 with -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would make me a few minutes to find the transcript reference, but my recollection of the witness's evidence was he wasn't sure where the Bandera Triangle was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't -- okay. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- let me perhaps put it this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You had -- I believe you indicated you weren't sure where the Bandera Triangle was, and when you were asked by Mr. Groome about this section where it says DutchBat not allowed to enter the area for their safety, you said you suspected that it was due to the Bosnian Serbs. Perhaps that's a more accurate recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following, that we take a break and we look at the source exactly what the witness said so that we have the transcript ready. Mr. Smith, you are invited to follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before we take the break, as matters stand now, still no need for re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Possibly one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Possibly one question. I might have one or two questions as well, which means that after the break, Mr. Ivetic, you would have most of the time but not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll keep that in mind, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to say something quickly with respect to the next witness. On the 23rd of January I raised a disclosure issue at transcript page 7275 to 76. I want to inform the Chamber and Defence counsel that the three documents that I mentioned we have permission now to disclose them and they will be disclosed within the hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We take a break and we will resume at 17 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have during the break located the transcript reference. And, sir, I will read for you and hopefully you can follow in today's transcript the exact words used. In your direct examination questioning by Mr. Groome at page 7336 of the transcript, from line 13 through line 22, it is recorded as follows: "Q. Now, further down in paragraph 5 of this report, we see the following sentence: "'DutchBat are not allowed to enter that area,' this is a reference again to Bandera Triangle, 'because of our safety. We can't investigate the number.' "Do you know if the determination that it was too unsafe for DutchBat to move around the enclave was a decision made by DutchBat or a restriction placed on their movement by the VRS? "A. My understanding at the time is they were being restricted in their movement by the VRS." Now, that was your testimony in the direct examination. I would like to have that in mind while we re-read paragraph 5 of this document in its entirety. "The number of BiH soldiers that are taken POW by the BSA is not known yet, but General Mladic told the UNMO team and the CO of DutchBat that the BiH are having several hundreds of dead soldiers in the area of the Bandera Triangle. He also asked the CO of DutchBat to contact those BiH soldiers and inform them that it is not the general's intention to kill any more soldiers of the BiH. They only have to surrender and hand over their weapons, because we, the UNMO team and DutchBat, are not allowed to enter that area because of our safety. We can't investigate the numbers. The CO of DutchBat told the general that he will try to contact the BiH through the HQ Sector North-east because the CO has no more contact with the BiH anymore." Now, in your direct examination, the assumption was the soldiers, the BiH soldiers in the Bandera Triangle were dead. I ask you, sir, wouldn't it then be illogical for General Mladic to tell the DutchBat and the UNMO to inform these soldiers in the Bandera Triangle to turn over their weapons, and would not a more logical reading of this be that there are still armed soldiers, perhaps dead, perhaps also live ones, in the triangle and that these are the ones that are being asked to turn over their weapons? Would you permit that that was a more logical reading of this paragraph than you and Mr. Groome had indicated during the direct examination?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it is illogical, as written, that he's -- it says that there are dead there, and then it says contact these soldiers. Now, whether this is someone writing in his second language, I don't know. It probably is, but I'm -- I don't know the author of the report. But there was a statement that -- and this place, the Bandera Triangle, there are several hundreds of dead soldiers. That seems to be one idea. And then there is an idea that there should be a contact with BiH soldiers. Now, whether these are in the triangle, wherever that is or was, or whether they are scattered amongst the dead ones and are still alive, I don't know. And I don't know enough of the author and his circumstances to be sure of how to interpret it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And there's one more concept and it's the concept of the inability of the UNMO and the DutchBat to enter that area, i.e., the Bandera Triangle because of their safety, and your answer said that it was your understanding at the time that they were being restricted in their movements by the VRS. Do you have a basis for that or were you just merely making a supposition?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That I am -- understand that that was the case once they were all holed up in Potocari and the -- the enclaves had collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we still have the witness statement of Mr. Koster on the right, I direct your attention to the last paragraph of this page, which continues on through the next page, and I'll read it for you so that we it all in the right line -- frame of thought. It says: "At the end of January 1995, the Muslim fighters wanted us to keep out of a certain part of the enclave. Major Franken and eight soldiers of the Reconnaissance Platoon endeavoured to enter this area in order to enforce the conditions of freedom of movement. When they did so, they were taken hostage. I believe that Zulfo, a subordinate commander in the Muslim forces, was responsible for this hostage-taking. I never saw this 'Zulfo.' He was one of Naser Oric's commanders. I later heard that there was an internal power struggle between these two men. "When this happened, Major Boering and van Alphen went to negotiate and were also taken hostage by BiH fighters. In total about 75 to 100 men were taken hostage. These men were taken hostage when they were on stand-by near what is known as the Bandera Triangle. This was in the western part of the enclave." Sir, do you recall hearing a reporting of such incidents occurring in the Bandera Triangle during your tenure as BH commander?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this reference in paragraph 5 of the document on our left could be a reference to the fact that since this incident from January of 1995, both the UNMOs and the DutchBat stayed out of the Bandera Triangle due to their own safety not because of the VRS but because of what the army BiH had done in January?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't draw that conclusion. The situation had materially changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, you had testified that there was a breakout of -- attempted break out of BiH forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- you're supposed not to interrupt the witness if he's in the middle of his answer. The situation had materially changed you said, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In January you have one situation, and by the time when the paragraph 5 of the report -- UNMO report is being drafted, the enclave has fallen and there are several hundreds of dead soldiers being reported in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall your testimony during your examination by Mr. Groome that there had been an attempted breakout of armed BiH soldiers from the enclave in the direction of the north-west? And this is from transcript page 7331 and 7332 of our trial transcript.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yet at that time you didn't know where the Bandera Triangle is. Now, knowing from Lieutenant Koster that's in the western part of the enclave, do you now permit that the possibility that the forces that were attempting to break out, the BiH forces were actually in the Bandera Triangle and were still there, or do you perhaps not know?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we -- the Bandera Triangle, I don't know where it is. I don't recall it being a phrase or description being used at all in my time in command. It's introduced to me for the first time in this examination. The breakout not only was attempted but it occurred, and it occurred in my memory to the north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'd like to move to another document, and I'd like to turn to -- first of all, in your statement, at paragraph 86 of the same, you indicate that you were personally involved in getting some Serb liaison officers out of Gornji Vakuf. That would be page 21 of the English, page 17 of the B/C/S of P785, marked for identification. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was certainly said it was to happen. I wasn't personally involved in their movement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the -- was the idea of such an action positively or negatively received by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 1D576 briefly. While we wait for that, sir, that is a document from the state security department centre of the Ministry of Interior of the MUP of Republika Srpska, dated April 18, 1995, and I have to present to you the information of the second paragraph that appears to relate to the same incidents. First of all, was the Gornji Vakuf incidents you are talking about in April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was about then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here in this document, the second paragraph says as follows: "During his stay in Kiseljak, our source heard from a Croat from Novi Travnik who was on a visit to Kiseljak that the withdrawal of VRS, Army of Republika Srpska, liaison officers from Vakuf, which is under the control of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had been ordered by the commander of UNPROFOR forces in the former Yugoslavia, General Smith. This was done in order to make it possible for the Croatian Army Main Staff to provide assistance in military hardware to the so-called Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. More precisely, to bring ten VBR multiple rocket launchers and five or six tanks from Croatia for the needs of an offensive by the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the general area of Vlasic during that period as well as for further offensive operations by the Muslim army aimed at linking up the zones of responsibility of the 5th and 7th Corps of the army of so-called Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Did in fact or do you have information that upon your actions to remove the VRS liaison officers, these heavy weapons were transferred by the army of Croatia to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this happening at all and that wasn't the reason I returned the liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you exclude the possibility that the army of Croatia in fact did undertake to take advantage of your actions and to make this transfer?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exclude the possibility, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was any complaint about this ever brought to your attention while you were at BH command?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What, that I returned the liaison officers or that the -- there'd been this --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The transfer?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the transfer of equipment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The transfer of equipment.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall a complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this document at this time as the next available 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D576 shall be assigned Exhibit D144. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D144 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 1D579 briefly. And while we wait for that, sir, this is a document authored by Brigadier General Nikolai sent to General Rasim Delic of the BiH forces the 9th of July, 1995, and I'd like -- first of all, do you recall one of your subordinates sending such a letter to General Delic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I saw this letter subsequently. I didn't -- I wasn't there when this was initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can look at the last two paragraphs and it says: "Our main consideration is the safety of the peacekeeping forces. Our forces will not retake the observation posts until the UNPROFOR Staff considers it safe to do so. The attempts of your forces to keep the observation posts in their place and attack the members of the withdrawing peacekeeping forces have only rendered the already dangerous and unstable situation even more complicated." Do you recall, sir, that during this time period you had information that the BiH forces had attacked UNPROFOR that were attempting to disengage from observation posts in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it in terms of that type of activity that one UNPROFOR soldier was actually killed by the ABiH forces?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Just let me finish reading the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's covered in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you can clarify for us. The last paragraph seems to imply that during this time period air strikes were called against the Serbs for the self-defence of UNPROFOR personnel but had not taken place due to target identification. Do you recall that situation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall. As I say, I wasn't there. But it doesn't say it's against the Serbs at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, it says in response to your two other requests, I can inform you that NATO air support was provided during combat. Do you suppose --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you can deduce that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah. And do --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I'm assuming that's two other requests for information as opposed to requests for air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess both readings are possible, sir. Do you recall if the -- if the BiH forces were ever threatened with air strikes following this set of instances?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, no. And I don't think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that be introduced as the next 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D579 shall be assigned Exhibit D145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. You've got five minutes left, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can call up P792, and this is a document authored by you which was discussed in direct examination and sent to the Serb side protesting, and it's dated the 26th of June, 1995. Once we receive the same, I would like to focus on the middle -- or the one, two, three -- fourth paragraph from the top. And here, sir, you are protesting the attacks on the civilian population and also attacks on observation posts by the Serbs, and you say in the next paragraph: "I cannot tolerate attacks on my troops, and I want to remind you once again that I will not hesitate to respond in self-defence." And the question I have for you, sir, is we've talked now these last few days and we've seen during this same time-period the ABiH was attacking observation posts, performing attacks attacking the civilian population in Serb villages around Srebrenica. Why is it that you, sir, are only threatening the Bosnian Serb side for activities that the Bosnian Muslim side is doing as well?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not entirely correct in what you've stated. My memory of the killing of the Dutch soldiers as they were trying to withdraw from the observation posts. It wasn't that the observation posts were being attacked by the ABiH. And the point about the threat to the attacking of civilian areas, it goes straight back to the exclusion zones and the safe area policy. The area that I was responsible for with the civilians in it was the safe area, and that was where I -- my focus, if you like, was. And finally, we were not allowed into the Bosnian Serb areas and had no knowledge other than Bosnian Serb reporting of actions that were taking place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that during this time period the only casualties in Srebrenica on the part of UNPROFOR were the soldier that was killed by ABiH fire and that none were casualties of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go back to Markale just briefly. Do you recall a Colonel Demurenko who was Chief of Staff of Sector Sarajevo and who presented a press conference basically challenging the official version of the Markale II incident?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your office take any steps upon that press conference to investigate the claims made by Colonel Demurenko and to further supplement its own findings as to the Markale II incident that we've talked about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We disagreed with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to investigate Colonel Demurenko's findings and to --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- again, my recall is that argument was supplied to us and we disagreed with it. It was, as I remember, an example of not including all the evidence to arrive at a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Isn't it also a fact, sir, that Colonel Demurenko visited all the sites where your -- where the UNMO team's bearings would have been the firing locations based upon the various potential charges that could be attached to a 120-millimetre mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall that he did that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that he claimed that he did that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that particular bit either.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did any of the teams performing investigations for either you or any other UN entities in reaching the determination for Markale attempt to go and locate and visit potential firing positions to determine if the mortar shells could possibly have been fired from there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we were allowed to do that by the Bosnian Serbs but I couldn't produce you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir I put it --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the chapter and verse of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in your telephone conversation with General Mladic he invited you to form a joint commission to investigate everything and he turned it down?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. It was my business to make the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So it's not a matter of the Serbs not permitting you, it was you not permitting the Serbs to have the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could Mr. Ivetic please assist me with the reference in the telephone call where Mr. Mladic invited General Smith to visit the specific locations? I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be that it's the interpretation apparently of inviting to form a joint committee would entail, would include, Mr. Ivetic, that is what I understand, that that joint commission would then have to -- yes. There appears to be a problem as far as Mr. Mladic is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apparently there is a problem with the translation, Your Honours. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will verify that. If we slow down, Mr. Ivetic, that may assist the translation as well. It seems, Mr. Groome, that it's a different interpretation of what it means to invite for a joint commission which would then most likely result in going to the area and there is no literal permission given to enter the Bosnian Serb territory. That seems to be the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. That's what I intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. -- you've past your last minute more or less, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I get an answer to my last question that was posed then, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please put it again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me read it back to you. It's at line 10, 11: "Am I correct, sir, it's not a matter of the Serbs not permitting you, it was you not permitting the Serbs to have that investigation?"

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the same thing, is it? I don't think we were allowed to travel independently into Bosnian Serb territory and that's not the same thing as a joint commission. And finally, I make the point that a mortar is a mobile weapon and it can be easily moved after it is fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Groome, you said one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, can you explain to the Chamber why it was you did not pursue General Mladic's suggestion that the investigation of Markale II be done in a joint commission?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can just take a moment to make a couple of notes, to make this as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose I divide it into the following: The first is that it was in my experience and reading the experience of my predecessors a common tactic of all parties, not only the Bosnian Serbs, when faced with these situations to arrive at some joint commission in which the whole thing would descend into yes, he did, no, he didn't, type of debate going long into the future if it arrives at a result at all. Secondly, as a result of the London Conference, the situation had changed as far as the exclusion zone regime was concerned, and the decision lay in equal part with the two military commanders, NATO and the UN, and at the time, I was the man for the UN, and I was required to make a decision. And at the London Conference, the decision to bomb had already, in effect, been made. It required that an attack by -- on a safe area. And so I was needing to establish whether this had actually occurred, and if so, who had attacked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few questions for you in relation to the Markale II incident. Could we have on the screen P785, English page 51, B/C/S page 40. That is paragraph 201 is of your statement, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got my pages in a muddle. One minute. 201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 201. Especially the end. Could you please read for yourself the last five, six, lines on from the Cymbeline ray car.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In a built-up area --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. It's --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just read it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood this part of your statement to be that if you fire in a built-up area, that you need a very high trajectory which would certainly have crossed the cut of the Cymbeline radar, whereas if you fire from a longer distance that you might have stayed below of that. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then in order to visualise it, could a sketch be put on the ELMO. I'm not a good sketcher, Mr. Smith. It should appear on your screen. I don't see it on my screen yet. There it is. Could you adjust it in such a way that ... I see it on the screen with the Registrar but not on my screen under the ELMO button. I apologise to all of those assisting us for the -- I asked it to be ready when I would put the questions, but for one reason or another.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we also have it? I have it under the video button at this moment, although could we focus and exclusively look on the screen despite whatever instructions do exist that we see the picture I so desperately tried to produce. Yes. I have it now on my screen and nothing else should be on our screen at this moment. Mr. Smith, I tried to make a sketch of a shell being fired in an urban area from nearby and from further away. You said you need a high trajectory. My question to you is what do you need? Do you need a steep trajectory or do you need a high trajectory?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me start. The point I think I was trying to make in this bit of the statement was that in a built-up area, you have to get the round, if I can point at the screen, to go up between the houses. Otherwise, you hit the houses on your way out, which isn't a good idea. So this would give you a more vertical shoot, because to make it -- to oversimplify, the maximum range is achieved at 45 degrees, and you can shorten the range by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you do not mind if I interrupt you. I understand all that. At the same time, you used -- I want this to remain on the screens. Yes. You said a high trajectory was an explanation why it should have been --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- caught by the Cymbeline. Now, on this sketch I do agree with you that you need a rather steep trajectory, first of all, to get out of the built-up area, and of course a corresponding steep angle of descent so that it lands not against the wall of a house but in a street, for example.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the steepness rather than the elevation is the real issue?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's the verticality of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you also agree with me that if I have a cut of the Cymbeline higher up that it doesn't make that much of a difference as shown in this sketch, that if you fire with a steep trajectory with a low charge because it doesn't have to travel very long, that it might well remain under the radar if it cuts a higher part of the area as shown -- as demonstrated in this sketch?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would depend upon the charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But you have not included the charge as an element of --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't include the charge. All I was talking about was the -- the -- I'll call it the steepness, yes, of the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for it to be caught by the radar, the elevation, the height is rather relevant than the steepness as we see here.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we now have the other sketch on the ELMO. Now, the scale here is slightly different, as you see it. What I did is make a sketch of a longer distance firing, because the suggestion was if you fire from a longer distance, the trajectory may be flatter and may not be caught by the radar. Would you agree with me that with such a flatter angle of firing, and of course a corresponding angle of descent, that the chance of landing in a street is by far lower because there's a fair chance that you hit roofs and/or other buildings, not landing in a street?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
